newsitem.title: USA: Clinton reading up on past inaugural addresses.
newsitem.headline: Clinton reading up on past inaugural addresses.

text.p: President Clinton is busily reading up on the inaugural addresses of past presidents entering their second term as he prepares for his own speech Monday.
Last weekend Clinton ordered up those speeches and has read a number of them in the search for ideas of how to make his own as spellbinding as possible.
Clinton, said White House spokesman Mike McCurry, wanted "to see how incumbent presidents upon re-inauguration have done the re-run -- how do you do a re-run and make it exciting?"

Probably the most famous second-term inaugural address was Abraham Lincoln's 1865 "Malice Toward None" speech as the country approached the end of the Civil War. Other second-termers include George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Woodrow Wilson, Franklin Roosevelt and Ronald Reagan.
Clinton has been spending a lot of time agonizing over the speech, reading what his speech-writers produce, sending them away with more ideas, and writing some on his own.
"I asked him, 'How is it going?' He said, 'it's getting there,'" McCurry said.
McCurry described the inaugural address as a "vision statement for America as we approach the 21st century."

It is unclear how long the typically verbose Clinton will speak on Monday after he is inaugurated at the Capitol. But he only spoke for 14 minutes at his 1993 inaugural and aides said he recently compared that speech to others in history and concluded it was on the short side.
